rules.summary: Montana law lists it as a survivor's right not to be billed for the sexual assault forensic exam or the evidence kit collection. The statute does not say whether the survivor's insurance may be billed.
rules.quote: a victim may not be billed for the cost of administering the sexual assault medical forensic examination or collecting evidence for the sexual assault evidence kit

rules.summary: When the state exam fund (FREPP) pays, the provider must take that as payment in full and cannot bill the survivor for the rest. Treatment of physical injuries from the assault is not part of the exam payment and may still be billed to the survivor (Crime Victim Compensation may cover it as a medical cost).
rules.quote: A healthcare provider must accept FREPP’s reimbursement rate as payment in full for covered services and may not submit any remaining balance to the survivor or commence civil actions against the survivor to recover the balance. Treatment of any physical injuries that may have occurred at the time of the sexual assault may still be billed to the survivor.

params.payer: local law enforcement agency where the offense occurred

rules.summary: The local law enforcement agency pays for the exam when it directed the exam or uses the evidence.
rules.quote: The local law enforcement agency within whose jurisdiction an alleged incident of sexual intercourse without consent, sexual assault, or incest occurs shall pay for the sexual assault medical forensic examination of a victim of the alleged offense when the examination is directed by the agency or when evidence obtained by the examination is used for the investigation, prosecution, or resolution of an offense.

params.payer: Montana Department of Justice (Forensic Rape Examination Payment Program), subject to available funds

rules.summary: Otherwise the Montana Department of Justice pays for the exam, as long as appropriated funds are available. This is how exams are paid when the survivor does not report to police.
rules.quote: The department of justice shall, as long as funds are available from an appropriation made for this purpose, pay for the sexual assault medical forensic examination of a victim of an alleged incident of sexual intercourse without consent, sexual assault, or incest if the cost is not the responsibility of a local law enforcement agency under subsection (1).

rules.summary: If the assault is not reported to police, the exam is paid by FREPP at the Montana Department of Justice, so a survivor can get an exam without reporting.
rules.quote: For cases that are not reported to law enforcement, the cost is paid by FREPP at the Montana Department of Justice.

rules.summary: FREPP pays providers up to $600 per exam, and only for exams done with a sexual assault evidence kit. The $600 is a limit on what the provider is paid; the provider cannot bill the survivor for the balance.
rules.quote: Exams administered without using a kit are not eligible. FREPP pays for the cost of a sexual assault exam up to a maximum of $600.

rules.summary: Crime Victim Compensation can pay up to $25,000 in benefits.
rules.quote: The CVC can pay up to $25,000 in benefits.
rules.pinpoint: Montana DOJ, Crime Victim Compensation page, Eligible Benefits

rules.summary: Counseling for secondary victims (certain family members, such as the parent or sibling of a minor sexual offense victim) is capped at $5,000 or 12 consecutive months per person, whichever comes first. This cap is for family members, not the primary victim.
rules.quote: Total payments made under subsections (9)(a) through (9)(d) may not exceed $5,000 or 12 consecutive months of treatment for each person, whichever occurs first.

rules.summary: Funeral and burial expenses are capped at $10,000, after other sources pay.
rules.quote: Reasonable funeral and burial expenses of the victim, not exceeding $10,000, must be paid if all other collateral sources have properly paid expenses but have not covered all expenses.

rules.summary: Reasonable doctor, hospital, and medicine costs for crime injuries are covered.
rules.quote: The claimant is entitled to be reimbursed for reasonable services by a physician or surgeon, reasonable hospital services and medicines, and other treatment approved by the office for the injuries suffered due to criminally injurious conduct.

rules.summary: Mental health counseling is covered for the victim and for eligible family members.
rules.quote: Mental health counseling benefits are available for primary and secondary victims
rules.pinpoint: Montana DOJ, Crime Victim Compensation page, Mental Health Costs

rules.summary: The program's list of medical costs includes prescription drugs, ambulance charges, and dental treatment.
rules.quote: Prescription drugs Ambulance charges Dental treatment
rules.pinpoint: Montana DOJ, Crime Victim Compensation page, Medical Costs

rules.summary: Dental treatment is listed as a covered medical cost.
rules.quote: Prescription drugs Ambulance charges Dental treatment
rules.pinpoint: Montana DOJ, Crime Victim Compensation page, Medical Costs

rules.summary: Lost wages are paid weekly when the injury causes a total loss of wages. The statute sets the weekly rate as a share of the victim's wages, capped at half the state's average weekly wage.
rules.quote: A claimant is entitled to weekly compensation benefits when the claimant has a total actual loss of wages due to injury as a result of criminally injurious conduct.

rules.summary: For a minor victim of a sexual offense, the parent or guardian can get mileage at the IRS rate (subject to the statute's per-person limits).
rules.quote: the parent or guardian of a minor who is a victim of criminally injurious conduct involving a sexual offense and who is not entitled to receive services under Title 41, chapter 3, is entitled to: (i) claim benefits under subsection (1); (ii) mileage at the rate allowed by the internal revenue service for the current year;

rules.summary: The program does not pay for stolen, damaged, or destroyed property (for example a phone). It may still pay for items such as eyeglasses, hearing aids, crutches, braces, and prosthetic devices.
rules.quote: No, the CVC program cannot pay for stolen, damaged, or destroyed property.  CVC may pay for items such as eyeglasses, hearing aids, crutches, braces, and prosthetic devices.

rules.summary: Clothing is listed as an ineligible non-medical expense.
rules.quote: Non-medical expenses, like clothing, motels , travel expenses, or legal fees
rules.pinpoint: Montana DOJ, Crime Victim Compensation page, Ineligible Benefits

rules.summary: Motels are listed as an ineligible non-medical expense.
rules.quote: Non-medical expenses, like clothing, motels , travel expenses, or legal fees
rules.pinpoint: Montana DOJ, Crime Victim Compensation page, Ineligible Benefits

rules.summary: Travel expenses are listed as ineligible. The statute does allow mileage for a parent or guardian of a minor sexual offense victim (listed separately as a covered transportation expense).
rules.quote: Non-medical expenses, like clothing, motels , travel expenses, or legal fees
rules.pinpoint: Montana DOJ, Crime Victim Compensation page, Ineligible Benefits

rules.summary: Legal fees are listed as an ineligible non-medical expense.
rules.quote: Non-medical expenses, like clothing, motels , travel expenses, or legal fees
rules.pinpoint: Montana DOJ, Crime Victim Compensation page, Ineligible Benefits

params.item: pain and suffering, inconvenience, physical impairment, nonbodily damage

rules.summary: No payment for pain and suffering, inconvenience, physical impairment, or nonbodily damage.
rules.quote: Compensation benefits are not payable for pain and suffering, inconvenience, physical impairment, or nonbodily damage.

params.item: missed work due to mental impairment

rules.summary: Lost wages are paid only for physical injury; missed work due to mental impairment is not covered.
rules.quote: CVC does not cover missed work due to mental impairment.
rules.pinpoint: Montana DOJ, Crime Victim Compensation page, Wage Loss

params.item: in-patient psychiatric care or chemical dependency counseling

rules.summary: In-patient psychiatric care and chemical dependency counseling are listed as ineligible.
rules.quote: In-patient psychiatric care or chemical dependency counseling
rules.pinpoint: Montana DOJ, Crime Victim Compensation page, Ineligible Benefits

params.extension: The office may extend the time for good cause shown (MCA 53-9-125(1)); ARM 23.15.103(2) says there is no good cause once a claim is more than two years past the latest allowed filing date.

rules.summary: File within 1 year of the crime. The office can extend this for good cause.
rules.quote: compensation may not be awarded unless the claim is filed with the office within 1 year after the day the criminally injurious conduct occurred causing the injury or death upon which the claim is based.

params.extension: Applies to sexual offenses against minors; the later of 1 year after the report or 1 year after age 18. Good cause extensions also apply.

rules.summary: For sexual offenses against minors, the deadline is 1 year after the report to police or child welfare, or 1 year after the victim turns 18, whichever is later.
rules.quote: Compensation in cases involving sexual offenses against minors may not be awarded unless the claim is filed with the office within 1 year after the day the criminally injurious conduct was reported to a law enforcement agency or an agency of the state responsible for provision of child welfare services, or within 1 year after the day the victim reaches 18 years of age, whichever occurs last.

rules.summary: A report to a law enforcement officer is required, made within 72 hours, unless the office finds good cause for the delay or the case is a sexual offense against a minor. Good cause factors in the administrative rules include the reasonableness of the delay and physical or mental incapacity. The statute lists no alternative to a police report for adult survivors. The forensic exam itself does not require a report.
rules.quote: Compensation may not be awarded unless the criminally injurious conduct resulting in injury or death was reported to a law enforcement officer. The report must be made within 72 hours after its occurrence, except in a case involving a sexual offense against a minor or when the office finds there was good cause for the failure to report within that time.

rules.summary: The program pays after insurance and other sources; payments are reduced by what those sources pay or could pay.
rules.quote: Compensation otherwise payable to a claimant must be reduced or denied to the extent the compensation benefits payable are or can be recouped from collateral sources.

rules.summary: The program is the payer of last resort, but it can pay deductibles and co-pays.
rules.quote: CVC is a payor of last resort. If you are covered by any kind of private or government benefit program, you must submit your expenses to that collateral source before you submit them to the CVC program. CVC benefits can be paid for your out-of-pocket expenses, including any required deductible or co-payment.
rules.pinpoint: Montana DOJ, Crime Victim Compensation page, Insurance and Collateral Sources

rules.summary: An award may be reduced or denied in proportion to the victim's contribution to the injury.
rules.quote: Compensation may be denied or reduced if the victim contributed to the infliction of death or injury with respect to which the claim is made. Any reduction in benefits under this subsection must be in proportion to what the office finds to be the victim's contribution to the infliction of death or injury.

rules.summary: An award may be denied or reduced if the claimant or victim does not fully cooperate with police and prosecutors.
rules.quote: The office, upon finding that the claimant or victim has not fully cooperated with appropriate law enforcement agencies or prosecuting attorneys, may deny or reconsider and reduce an award of compensation.

rules.summary: A tentative award can be paid early when the claimant faces financial hardship and a final award looks likely. No set amount.
rules.quote: If the office determines that the claimant will suffer financial hardship unless a tentative award is made and it appears likely that a final award will be made, an amount may be paid to the claimant, to be deducted from the final award or repaid by and recoverable from the claimant to the extent that it exceeds the final award.

rules.summary: Adult sexual assault is a listed crime type on the claim form.
rules.quote: [ ] Adult Sexual Assault
rules.pinpoint: Claim Form, Section C, Type of Crime

params.rule: Crimes in Montana regardless of residency; Montana residents injured where the local program does not compensate non-residents

rules.summary: Anyone hurt by a crime in Montana can apply, including non-residents. Montana residents hurt elsewhere can apply only if that state or country's program does not cover non-residents.
rules.quote: Benefits may be awarded to: Non-residents injured in Montana. Montana residents injured in a state or country in which the victim compensation program does not compensate non-residents.
rules.pinpoint: Montana DOJ, Request a Claim Form page

coverage.notes: Montana has no fixed dollar cap on lost wages for employed victims; MCA 53-9-128(1) pays 66 2/3% of wages up to one-half the state's average weekly wage, and 53-9-128(7)(a) caps victims who were employable but not employed at $100 per week. ARM 23.15.306(3) limits primary-victim counseling to 12 consecutive months or $2,000 with extensions available, but the same rule's secondary-victim limit ($2,000) has been superseded by the statute ($5,000), and the DOJ page names no primary-victim cap, so I did not encode a primary-victim counseling cap. I found no relocation, security, or minimum-loss provision. Neither the statute nor FREPP pages say whether the survivor's insurance may be billed for the exam.

researcher_notes: Total cap of $25,000 comes from the DOJ program page; the statute itself only caps death cases at $25,000 (MCA 53-9-128(5)). Reporting: adult survivors must report to law enforcement within 72 hours unless good cause is shown (ARM 23.15.103 lists factors such as the reasonableness of the delay and incapacity); there is no statutory alternative such as a forensic exam or advocate report. The exam itself does not require a report: unreported exams are paid by FREPP (MCA 46-15-411(2); DOJ FREPP page). ARM 23.15.402(1) (2005) says FREPP requires the exam within 72 hours and that the victim choose not to report; the current DOJ FREPP page does not repeat the 72-hour condition, so I left it out of the rules. MCA 46-15-411(3) and the FREPP page say treatment of physical injuries from the assault is not covered by the exam payment and may be billed to the survivor; CVC may still cover such medical costs under MCA 53-9-128(2). ARM rules were saved from Cornell LII because the Secretary of State ARM site is script-driven. Reviewer note: MCA 53-9-103(3)(b) and (6)(a) define criminally injurious conduct and victim in terms of bodily injury or death, while the DOJ page describes a primary victim as someone who suffered direct physical or emotional harm; a survivor without a physical injury should confirm eligibility with the office. MT-CAP-2 uses the non-standard param applies_to: secondary_victims; the $5,000 counseling cap does not apply to the primary victim under the statute.
